## Agenda {.smaller}

Two things every production agent runs on that no demo ever shows: a
budget, and a shared vocabulary.

- **Part 1: Tokenomics** -- what LLM calls cost, the levers that move the
  bill (caching, batching, routing), cost-per-task thinking, the
  open-weight vs frontier decision, and how to benchmark it on your own
  workload
- **Part 2: The semantic layer** -- ontologies and knowledge graphs,
  grounding text-to-SQL, why agents need machine-readable meaning, and
  the vendor race that broke out this year (AWS, Microsoft, Databricks,
  NVIDIA, and an Apache standard)
- Next week: fine-tuning, responsible AI, and the course close

# Part 1: Tokenomics

## What Is Tokenomics?

- **Tokenomics**: the economics of building on token-metered models
- Every LLM call is a purchase: you pay per **token in** and per
  **token out**
- Small design decisions (prompt length, model choice, retry policy)
  compound into the largest line item of a GenAI product
- The developer's job: deliver **required quality at the lowest
  cost-per-task**, never the lowest cost-per-token

## How API Pricing Works

- Providers price per **million tokens**, split three ways:

| Meter | What it covers | Typical relative price |
|-------|----------------|------------------------|
| **Input tokens** | Prompt: system, context, history, tools | Baseline |
| **Output tokens** | Generated completion | ~3-5x input |
| **Cached input tokens** | Previously seen prompt prefix | ~0.1-0.25x input |

- Consequence: **verbose outputs are the most expensive thing you can
  ask for**
- Batch and asynchronous tiers offer roughly 50% discounts for
  non-interactive work

## Cost Drivers in Real Applications {.smaller}

Everything this course built in weeks 5 to 11 shows up on the bill:

- **Context stuffing**: RAG chunks, long system prompts, full
  conversation history resent every turn
- **Tool schemas**: every tool definition rides along in *every* request
  -- week 6's MCP tool lists are input tokens
- **Agent loops**: one user request becomes many model calls (plan, act,
  reflect, retry) -- week 5's loop, priced
- **Reasoning tokens**: extended-thinking modes bill hidden intermediate
  tokens as output
- **Retries and fallbacks**: failures you pay for twice
- **Fan-out**: week 10's A2A delegation nests a full agent loop inside
  another agent's tool call; the bills nest the same way

## Anatomy of a Request's Cost

```text
cost = (input_tokens   x input_price)
     + (cached_tokens  x cached_price)
     + (output_tokens  x output_price)

task_cost = sum over requests per task   <- the number that matters
```

- Instrument **per-task token accounting** from day one; the week 7
  traces already carry the token counts
- An agent that makes 25 calls at $0.01 each is a $0.25 agent -- price
  it like one

## Lever 1: Prompt Caching

- Providers cache **stable prompt prefixes**: system prompt, tool
  schemas, few-shot examples, large documents
- Cache hits bill at a fraction of input price, and return faster
- Design rule: **stable content first, volatile content last** -- any
  change invalidates everything after it
- Biggest wins: agents (same system prompt and tools every call),
  long-document Q&A, chat with long history

## Lever 2: Batching

- **Batch APIs**: submit jobs asynchronously, get results within hours,
  pay about half price
- Ideal for: evaluation runs (week 7's eval suites belong here),
  document pipelines, embedding generation, nightly enrichment
- Self-hosted equivalent: **continuous batching** in vLLM and SGLang
  raises GPU utilization, so more tokens per dollar of compute (week 2)
- Ask of every workload: *does anyone need this answer in real time?*

## Lever 3: Model Routing and Cascades {.smaller}

- **Routing**: classify the request, send it to the cheapest model that
  can handle it
  - Small, fast models for extraction, classification, and easy traffic
  - Frontier models for the hard reasoning
- **Cascade**: try cheap first; escalate only on low confidence or
  failed validation
- **Model gateways** (LiteLLM, OpenRouter) centralize routing, fallback,
  and spend tracking
- You watched a real one get fixed: week 8's Meru case study was a
  2B-parameter router choosing among execution paths, tuned with a
  labeled set and a calibration pass
- Routing typically cuts spend far more than prompt tweaking -- most
  traffic is easy traffic

## More Cost Levers {.smaller}

- **Output discipline**: max-token limits, terse formats (JSON, not
  prose), "answer only" instructions
- **Context management**: summarize or truncate history; retrieve less
  but better
- **Distillation and fine-tuning**: move a high-volume narrow task from
  a frontier model to a small tuned model -- next week's lecture
- **Quantization** (self-hosted): more throughput per GPU (week 2)
- **Semantic response caching**: identical and near-identical questions
  answered from cache, zero tokens

## Cost-per-Task vs Cost-per-Token

- Cost-per-token comparisons across models mislead:
  - A cheaper model that needs 3 attempts and a human review costs more
  - A pricier model that one-shots the task may be the bargain
- Define the task, measure **end-to-end**: tokens x calls x success rate

```text
effective_cost = task_cost / success_rate
```

- This is why **evaluation (week 7) and tokenomics are inseparable**:
  you cannot optimize cost without measuring quality

## Build vs Buy Economics {.smaller}

| | **API (buy)** | **Self-hosted (build)** |
|---|--------------|------------------------|
| Cost shape | Pure variable (per token) | Fixed (GPUs) plus ops |
| Utilization risk | None | You pay for idle GPUs |
| Breakeven | Low or spiky volume | High, steady volume |
| Capability ceiling | Highest | High and rising |
| Version control | Provider-controlled | You pin the weights |
| Time to first call | Minutes | Days to weeks |
| Also consider | Data egress, rate limits | Talent, upgrades, model refresh cadence |

- Hidden costs run both ways: migration effort, prompt re-tuning when
  you swap models, egress
- Which means the cost question is really a **model choice** question,
  and that is the next section

# Open-Weight vs Frontier Models

## The Two Worlds of LLMs

- **Frontier, proprietary models**: weights never leave the lab; access
  by API only
- **Open-weight models**: weights are downloadable; run them anywhere
- The capability gap has narrowed, so the choice is now an engineering
  decision rather than a foregone conclusion
- Most real organizations end up with a **portfolio** of both

## The Landscape, Name Level {.smaller}

- **Frontier labs**: OpenAI (the GPT line), Anthropic (Claude in Opus,
  Sonnet, Haiku tiers), Google DeepMind (Gemini) -- strongest raw
  capability, managed safety, per-token pricing
- **Open-weight families**: Meta Llama (community license), DeepSeek
  (MoE and open reasoning models), Qwen (broad size range, strong
  coding), Mistral (Apache-2.0 and research licenses), GLM (Zhipu),
  OpenAI's gpt-oss line (Apache-2.0)
- Hugging Face Hub is the distribution channel in practice

::: {.hot-callout}
Model names and version numbers on this slide go stale within months.
Check the provider's own model page before you quote one in a design
review.
:::

## Open Weights Are Not Open Source {.smaller}

- **Open weights**: you get the trained parameters -- enough to run,
  fine-tune, and deploy
- **Open source**, in the strict sense: also the training code, the data
  recipe, and an OSI-approved license
- Most "open" LLMs release weights and inference code, **not** training
  data
- The [OSI Open Source AI Definition](https://opensource.org/ai)
  formalizes what qualifies

::: {.def-callout}
This matters for reproducibility, for auditability, and above all for
what your license permits you to ship.
:::

## Licenses: Read Before You Ship {.smaller}

- **Apache-2.0 and MIT** (many Mistral and Qwen releases, gpt-oss):
  permissive, commercial use, few strings
- **Community licenses** (Llama, for one): custom terms, acceptable-use
  policies, redistribution rules, and thresholds that kick in at very
  large deployments
- **Research-only licenses**: no commercial use at all
- Check the derivative rules: what applies to your fine-tunes and your
  distilled models?

::: {.hot-callout}
Legal review belongs in model selection, not after it. A license problem
found at launch is a rebuild.
:::

## What Each World Buys You {.smaller}

| **Frontier APIs** | **Open weights** |
|-------------------|------------------|
| Highest capability on the hardest tasks | **Control**: pin a version forever, no silent updates |
| Zero infrastructure to run or patch | **Privacy**: data never leaves your VPC |
| Fast access to new capabilities | **Customization**: full fine-tuning freedom (next week) |
| Managed safety and abuse monitoring | **Cost at scale**: sustained volume undercuts per-token pricing |
| Enterprise SLAs and data agreements | **Portability**: no lock-in across clouds and serving stacks |

- The middle path exists: managed open-weight endpoints (Bedrock, Azure
  AI Foundry, Together, Fireworks) give you the license and portability
  benefits without owning a GPU

## Model Selection Criteria {.smaller}

- **Task fit**: measured quality on *your* evals, not leaderboard rank
- **Modality and context**: text, vision, audio, and how much window you
  need
- **Latency budget**: interactive or batch
- **Cost model**: per-token API against amortized GPU spend
- **Data constraints**: residency, confidentiality, compliance regime
- **License**: permitted use, redistribution, derivatives
- **Ecosystem**: tooling, serving support, community fine-tunes

## Distillation and Right-Sizing {.smaller}

- **Knowledge distillation**: train a smaller student model on a
  stronger teacher's outputs; synthetic data from frontier models is now
  a standard training ingredient
- Reasoning distillation brought chain-of-thought behavior to small open
  models; the open ecosystem trails the frontier by months, not years
- **Small models, big roles**: 1B to 14B models do well at
  classification, extraction, routing, drafting -- the supply side of
  the routing lever, and what this course ran locally all semester
- A fine-tuned small model on a narrow task can match a general frontier
  model at a fraction of the cost (next week)

::: {.hot-callout}
Most frontier API terms restrict using their outputs to train a
competing model. Licenses, again.
:::

## Case Discussion

You are the architect. Which way, and why?

- A healthcare startup summarizing patient notes under HIPAA
- A consumer app doing 50M simple classifications a day
- An internal coding agent on a bank's proprietary codebase

Defend your choice on capability, privacy, cost, and license grounds.

# Measure, Then Decide

## From Cost to Benchmarking

- You cannot reason about tokenomics without **measured** performance
- Benchmarking answers, for *your* workload:
  - What does a request **cost**?
  - How **fast** is it (latency)?
  - How **much** can the system handle (throughput)?
  - Is the output **good enough** (accuracy)?
- The week 7 lesson carries: public leaderboards start the conversation;
  your own eval set ends it

## The Metrics That Matter

| Metric | Definition | Who cares |
|--------|-----------|-----------|
| **TTFT** | Time to first token | Interactive UX |
| **TPOT / ITL** | Time per output token | Streaming smoothness |
| **E2E latency** | Full request round trip | Batch and agent steps |
| **Throughput** | Tokens/sec or requests/min | Capacity planning |
| **Cost per 1M tokens** | Dollars normalized to volume | Finance |
| **Accuracy** | Task-specific quality score | Everyone |

## Latency Percentiles

- Never report averages alone -- LLM latency is long-tailed
- Report **p50 / p90 / p99**:
  - p50 is the typical experience
  - p99 is what your angriest users see, and what the SLA is written
    against
- Tail latency worsens under load (queueing, batching effects); measure
  at realistic **concurrency**, not with one sequential client
- Agent pipelines compound tails: 5 sequential calls at p90 each is
  close to a coin flip of at least one slow step

## Benchmarking Methodology {.smaller}

1. **Fix the workload**: real prompt and response length distributions
   from your app, not synthetic short prompts
2. **Sweep concurrency**: 1 to N clients; find where latency degrades
3. **Measure everything per run**: TTFT, TPOT, E2E, throughput, errors,
   dollars
4. **Hold accuracy constant**: a faster config that degrades quality is
   not faster, it is worse
5. **Repeat runs**; report percentiles with configs pinned (model
   version, quantization, instance)

Tools: [MLPerf](https://mlcommons.org/benchmarks/) for hardware,
[Ray LLMPerf](https://github.com/ray-project/llmperf) for load-testing
endpoints, and FMBench (next slide) for the full price-performance
picture.

## FMBench {.smaller}

[FMBench](https://github.com/aws-samples/foundation-model-benchmarking-tool)
benchmarks foundation models where they actually run:

- Deployments on SageMaker, Bedrock, EKS, and EC2; open-source,
  proprietary, and third-party models
- **Performance and cost in one run**: latency, throughput, and cost per
  request per instance type
- **LLM-judge evaluation**: a panel of judges scores relevance,
  correctness, coherence -- quality and cost measured on the same run,
  which is exactly the cost-per-task view
- **Bring your own dataset**: benchmark on your domain data, so the
  price-performance numbers reflect your task and not a leaderboard's
- Finding that recurs: the cheapest instance per hour is rarely the
  cheapest per token; the frontier must be **measured, not assumed**

# Part 2: The Semantic Layer

## Why Structure Knowledge at All?

- LLMs are fluent but **ungrounded**: they do not know *your* entities,
  relationships, or business definitions
- Vector RAG retrieves **similar text**, not **connected facts**
- Many real questions are relational: *"Which customers of our top
  supplier are also vendors?"*
- Structured knowledge gives agents something vectors cannot:
  **explicit, traversable, auditable relationships**

## Ontologies: the Vocabulary of a Domain

- An **ontology** is a formal specification of a domain:
  - **Classes** (types of things): `Person`, `Company`, `Drug`
  - **Properties** (attributes): `foundedYear`, `dosage`
  - **Relationships**: `worksFor`, `treats`, `acquiredBy`
  - **Constraints**: a `Person` `worksFor` a `Company`, never the
    reverse
- It encodes the *rules of what can be said* about a domain
- Standards: **RDF** (triples), **RDFS**, **OWL** (W3C)

## Triples and Knowledge Graphs {.smaller}

The atomic unit is the **triple**: *(subject, predicate, object)*

```text
(Bohr,       bornIn,           Copenhagen)
(Bohr,       collaboratedWith, Heisenberg)
(Heisenberg, developed,        UncertaintyPrinciple)
```

- Triples compose into a **knowledge graph**: nodes are entities, edges
  are typed relationships. Ontology = the schema; knowledge graph = the
  instance data
- Famous examples: Google Knowledge Graph, Wikidata, biomedical KGs
- Two dominant data models: **RDF / SPARQL** (W3C standards, formal
  reasoning) and **labeled property graphs / Cypher** (pragmatic,
  developer-friendly: Neo4j, Memgraph)
- KGs excel at **multi-hop questions**: follow edges instead of hoping
  chunks co-occur

## Vector RAG vs Graph RAG {.smaller}

You built both sides of this table in the week 4 labs:

| | **Vector RAG** | **Graph RAG** |
|---|---------------|---------------|
| Retrieval | Nearest-neighbor over embeddings | Graph traversal queries |
| Strength | Large unstructured corpora | Highly connected, relational data |
| Multi-hop | Weak: chunks must co-occur | Native: follow edges |
| Provenance | Similar chunks | Explicit paths, auditable |

- Not either/or: hybrid systems retrieve from both and fuse
- The graph-rag lab's pipeline was the standard one: ingest, LLM entity
  extraction, LLM relationship extraction, merge and dedupe, load, then
  traverse at query time

## Microsoft GraphRAG {.smaller}

[Microsoft GraphRAG](https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/) is the
open-source methodology that pushed past naive graph construction:

- LLM-based entity and relationship extraction, with descriptions
- **Community detection** (the Leiden algorithm) clusters the graph into
  hierarchical communities; an LLM writes a **summary report per
  community**
- Two search modes: **local** (start from matched entities, expand to
  neighbors and sources -- "what did X do?") and **global** (map-reduce
  over community summaries -- "what are the main themes?")
- Global search answers corpus-level questions that vector RAG
  structurally cannot
- The costs are real: every chunk passes through the LLM at indexing;
  entity resolution is hard ("IBM" vs "Big Blue"); freshness requires
  re-indexing. Use it when questions are relational or corpus-global

## From Documents to Databases

- Graph RAG structures **unstructured text**
- The other half of enterprise knowledge lives in **structured data**:
  warehouses, lakes, transactional stores
- LLMs face the same grounding problem there:
  - Which table is the *real* revenue table?
  - What does "active customer" mean, precisely?
- Enter the **semantic layer**

## The Semantic Layer {.smaller}

A **semantic layer** sits between raw data and consumers, defining:

- **Metrics**: `revenue = sum(order_total) where status = 'complete'`
- **Dimensions**: time, region, product hierarchies
- **Entities and joins**: how tables relate
- **Business definitions**: one agreed meaning of "churn", "active
  user", "margin"

Consumers -- BI tools, notebooks, and **agents** -- query *concepts*,
not tables. The established tools: dbt Semantic Layer / MetricFlow,
Cube, AtScale, Looker's LookML.

## Text-to-SQL Without Grounding Fails {.smaller}

Week 4's sql-rag lab met this head-on:

- Raw schema to LLM: hundreds of tables, cryptic column names, no
  definitions
- The model guesses joins, invents filters, picks the wrong "revenue"
  column
- Answers come back **plausible and wrong** -- the most dangerous
  failure mode in analytics
- With a semantic layer, the flow changes: the agent finds the `revenue`
  **metric** in the catalog (definition, valid dimensions), emits a
  metric query, and the layer compiles correct, governed SQL
- One definition of revenue means **consistent answers everywhere**:
  text-to-SQL goes from *schema guessing* to *definition lookup*

## Ontology vs Semantic Layer

| | Ontology / KG | Semantic layer |
|---|--------------|----------------|
| Domain | Entities and relationships in the world | Metrics and dimensions in the warehouse |
| Data shape | Graph (triples, property graph) | Relational (tables, cubes) |
| Query | SPARQL / Cypher | Metric queries compiled to SQL |
| Answers | "How are things connected?" | "What is the number, precisely?" |

Both are **machine-readable meaning** -- the connective tissue agents
need. The vendors have noticed, which is the next five slides.

## Why Agents Need a Semantic Layer {.smaller}

- **Determinism**: agents ground free-text requests in governed
  definitions instead of improvising SQL
- **Trust**: an answer traceable to a metric definition or a graph path
  is auditable; a raw LLM answer is not
- **Access control**: the layer enforces row- and column-level policy --
  the agent never touches raw tables (week 11's fine-grained
  authorization, applied to data)
- **Reuse**: one semantic model serves dashboards, notebooks, and every
  agent
- **MCP fit**: expose the semantic layer or KG as an MCP server, and any
  agent queries concepts as tools (week 6)

## AWS: Context Ontology Accelerator {.smaller}

[Context Ontology Accelerator](https://github.com/aws/context-ontology-accelerator)
(open source, Apache-2.0, July 2026):

- Builds a **machine-readable ontology of your business**: products,
  customers, policies, and the rules that define how they operate
- The workflow is AI-drafted, human-approved: it connects to your
  structured and unstructured sources, **drafts an ontology with AI**,
  and your domain experts review, edit, and approve every element
- Serves governed answers to agents, turning months of manual ontology
  authoring into days
- The roadmap folds it into **AWS Context** as a managed, user-defined
  ontology capability
- The pitch in one line: stop stuffing context into prompts; build an
  ontology that owns it

## Microsoft: Fabric IQ {.smaller}

[Fabric IQ](https://community.fabric.microsoft.com/blog/fbc_fabricupdatesblogs/fabric-iq-the-shared-context-layer-for-ai-agents-and-real-time-applications/5191678)
(GA at Build 2026; the ontology item still in preview):

- Layers an **ontology over OneLake and Power BI semantic models**:
  entities, relationships, natural-language rules, and live data
  bindings
- One source of business meaning, many consumers: Fabric data agents,
  operations agents, Foundry IQ, Copilot Studio, and **any MCP client**
  read the same ontology
- The operational angle is distinctive: agents do not just answer from
  the ontology, they **monitor what is happening and act on it**
- Microsoft's bet: the semantic model you already maintain for BI
  becomes your agents' source of truth

## Databricks: Unity Catalog Semantics {.smaller}

Databricks delivers the semantic layer through
[Unity Catalog](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/business-semantics/):

- **Metric views**: SQL-native, governed metric definitions that
  separate what you measure from how you slice it -- and they now flow
  into Power BI too
- **Business glossaries** attach agreed definitions to catalog objects
- **Genie Ontology** (gated public preview) adds inferred context and
  authority ranking on top
- Genie agents answer from data registered in Unity Catalog, using the
  attached metadata plus an author-curated knowledge store
- The through-line: one governed set of definitions flowing to BI,
  apps, and agents alike

## NVIDIA: Auto Ontology {.smaller}

[Auto Ontology](https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology) (open source,
Python):

- A framework for building a **semantic, graph-based reasoning layer
  over enterprise data**
- Four verbs: **discover** (generate an ontology from database
  metadata), **ground** (give agents trusted meaning for metrics,
  entities, relationships), **expose** (serve context through **MCP**,
  CLI, and API), **learn** (fold certified corrections and usage back
  in, so shared context improves with every question)
- People refine and certify the generated definitions -- the same
  AI-drafts, humans-approve shape as the AWS accelerator
- Works with NVIDIA NIM endpoints and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint

## The Standard: Apache Ossie {.smaller}

The missing piece was interchange -- every vendor's semantic model in
its own format:

- **Open Semantic Interchange (OSI)**, launched September 2025 by
  Snowflake with Salesforce, dbt Labs, BlackRock, and RelationalAI:
  a vendor-neutral YAML spec for metrics, dimensions, datasets, and
  relationships
- v1.0 shipped January 2026; in July 2026 the project entered the
  Apache Incubator as
  [Apache Ossie](https://www.snowflake.com/en/blog/apache-ossie-open-semantic-interchange-incubator/),
  with 50+ contributors and reference converters (dbt MetricFlow,
  Apache Polaris, Snowflake semantic models)
- Why it matters for agents: definitions written once move between the
  platforms on the previous slides instead of being trapped in one
- The week 6 pattern repeating: first MCP standardized the tools, now
  Ossie is trying to standardize the **meaning**

## Design Checklist for a Grounded Agent Stack {.smaller}

1. Which questions are **relational**? Those want the knowledge graph
2. Which questions are **quantitative**? Those want the semantic layer
3. Which are **lookup-shaped**? Plain vector RAG is enough
4. Define the **ontology and metric definitions first**; extraction and
   SQL generation follow
5. Expose each layer as a **tool over MCP** with clear, typed contracts
6. Log every traversal and query for **auditability** (week 7)

The week 4 labs built numbers 1 and 3 by hand; the vendor platforms on
the last five slides are selling you number 2 at enterprise scale.

## Key Takeaways {.smaller}

- Tokens are the unit of spend; output costs more than input, which
  costs more than cached -- design prompts accordingly
- The big levers are architectural: **caching, batching, routing** --
  and optimize **cost-per-task at target quality**, never cost-per-token
- Build vs buy is a utilization question; **open weights are not open
  source**, and the license decides what you can ship
- Benchmark with **your workload**, report **percentiles under
  concurrency**, keep accuracy in the loop
- Ontologies define what can be said; knowledge graphs hold what is
  known; the semantic layer is the **metrics ontology of the warehouse**
- Agents need machine-readable meaning, and 2026 is the year the
  vendors agreed: AWS, Microsoft, Databricks, and NVIDIA all shipped a
  semantic context layer, and the interchange format went to Apache
